newsitem.title: USA: Disney, Sesame Street toys make '10 worst' list.
newsitem.headline: Disney, Sesame Street toys make '10 worst' list.

text.p: Watch it. Bert, Slinky Dog and Winnie-the-Pooh are out to get you.
Toys based on these characters have made a consumer group's 10 worst toys list, which points out hazards that can be posed to children by even the most seemingly benign playthings.

Sesame Street's Bert, Disney's Slinky Dog from "Toy Story" and Winnie-the-Pooh join seven other toys on the annual list, compiled by Boston lawyer Ed Swartz, who heads the World Against Toys Causing Harm Inc. (WATCH).
Other losers include Hasbro Inc.'s Star Wars Electronic Luke Skywalker Lightsaber and its Nerf Chainblazer & Perceptor Blaster toys.

Swartz told reporters the Lightsaber, a 3-foot-long stick made of plastic, could be used as a bat or sword, saying, "I'd like to meet a child who won't jab this into something ... with a toy like this it's a weapon."

He called a Nerf toys that shoot darts, "an automatic, rapid-fire zip gun. They're weapons, play weapons, but weapons nonetheless and it's time to disarm the nursery," said Swartz, who has campaigned for safer toys since 1965.
But Hasbro spokesman Wayne Charness said, "I think a far better judge of these toys is the market. ... These are very successful toys and we have had no reported safety concerns with either of them."

Surrounded by about 100 New England children -- including tow-headed William Cookston, 5, of Clifton, Maine, who said he lost his right eye after playing with a Sky Dancer, a winged doll designed to be catapulted into the air from a launcher -- Swartz's adult-aged son James said, "There are a number of warnings on this product. You have to start wondering why it's on the market in the first place."

Topping the list of dangerous toys, however, was Disney's Toy Story Slinky Dog Pull Toy, made by James Industries Inc. of Hollidaysburg, Pa. The toy's body contains a plastic "slinky," or coil, that WATCH said could be stretched to 8-1/2 feet in length. The toy, designed for those 18 months and up, also has a 21-inch long string. Both elements create the potential for strangulation should the child put the slinky around his or her neck, WATCH said.

James Industries Inc. referred calls seeking comment to the Toy Manufacturers of America (TMA), the New York-based trade group that represents 290 producers and importers of toys in the United States.

TMA in a statement said they welcome information from individuals who identify unsafe toys so that corrective action may be taken. "However, we are dismayed that unqualified persons consistently fail to notify TMA, toy manufacturers, retailers of the proper authorities when they identify a perennial violation ...
"More to the point, these lists are meaningless and frightening to thoughtful consumers," said TMA.

Perhaps among the most surprising toys to make the list are Sesame Street's Pull Back N'Go Jet Plane, made by Tyco Toys and piloted by Bert, and "Christopher Robin Gives Pooh a Party," published by Dutton Children's Books.
WATCH found the propeller on Bert's moulded plastic plane could be easily removed to expose a half-inch metal pin that could harm an unsuspecting child.

Tyco said in a statement that the toy "meets or exceeds all ASTM (American Standard Testing and Materials) and other safety standards. ... Since its introduction in 1988, we have not received a single complaint about his product."

As for the A.A. Milne classic, this edition comes with a small, pewter Winnie-the-Pooh charm attached to a 24-inch long ribbon necklace. WATCH notes this version of the childhood classic contains no warnings, instructions or age recommendations and the charm could easily be swallowed.

"It is not a book or item for small children, nor has it been marketed as such," said Tim Moses of Dutton. "In the four years (this book has been on the market), we have never received a safety complaint and we deny that there is any danger to the book's intended readership. It's for children 5 to 10."
